title: The Qubit and the Bloch Sphere
intro: Every pure state of a qubit, up to global phase, is a point on the unit sphere. The coordinates of that point are the three expectation values $\langle X\rangle$, $\langle Y\rangle$, $\langle Z\rangle$, which is why the QRC pages can treat a qubit state as a vector of features.

blocks.text: A qubit state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$ has four real parameters. Normalisation removes one and the irrelevant global phase another, leaving two. Choosing them as angles gives

blocks.caption: θ and φ are the polar and azimuthal angles of a point on the unit sphere.

blocks.text: The north pole ($\theta = 0$) is $\vert0\rangle$, the south pole is $\vert1\rangle$, and the equator holds the equal superpositions: $\vert+\rangle$ at $\phi = 0$, $\vert+i\rangle$ at $\phi = \pi/2$, $\vert-\rangle$ at $\phi = \pi$. The half-angles are not a typo: orthogonal states, which are 90° apart as vectors in the state space, sit at opposite poles, 180° apart on the sphere.

blocks.alt: A sphere with |0> at the north pole and |1> at the south pole, |+> and |-> on the x axis, |+i> and |-i> on the y axis, and a blue state vector |psi> at polar angle theta from the z axis and azimuth phi from the x axis.
blocks.caption: The Bloch sphere. A pure state is a point on the surface; θ sets the balance between |0⟩ and |1⟩, φ the relative phase.

blocks.text: The Bloch vector is the vector of expectation values
The Cartesian coordinates of the point are

blocks.caption: The Bloch vector. For a pure state its length is 1.

blocks.text: So the geometry and the measurement statistics are the same thing. Knowing the three numbers $\langle X\rangle$, $\langle Y\rangle$, $\langle Z\rangle$ fixes the state, and the overlap between two states is set by the angle between their Bloch vectors: $\vert\langle\psi\vert\varphi\rangle\vert^2 = (1 + \vec r\cdot\vec r\,')/2$. Mixed states (Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states)) fill the inside of the ball, with $\vert\vec r\vert < 1$; the centre is the maximally mixed state.
The QRC input state on the sphere

The reset encoding of the Fujii–Nakajima reservoir writes $s\in[0,1]$ as $\sqrt{1-s}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt s\,\vert1\rangle$. Its amplitudes are real and non-negative, so $\phi = 0$: the input moves along the meridian in the $xz$ plane, from the north pole ($s = 0$) through $\vert+\rangle$ ($s = 1/2$) to the south pole ($s = 1$), with Bloch vector $(2\sqrt{s(1-s)}, 0, 1 - 2s)$. Two functions of $s$, one linear and one with a square root, which is exactly the nonlinearity budget analysed on Expressivity and Universality (#/qrc/theory/expressivity-and-universality).

Output of the run: the poles and the equatorial states land on the axes as expected; $\theta = \pi/3$, $\phi = \pi/4$ gives $(0.612, 0.612, 0.5)$; every pure state has length 1.000. For the input encoding, $s = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1$ give $(0, 0, 1)$, $(0.866, 0, 0.5)$, $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 0, -1)$.

Try it: drag θ from 0 to 180 and watch $P(1) = \sin^2(\theta/2)$ grow in the bars while the vector travels from the north pole to the south pole. Then move φ and check that the bars do not move. Setting θ = 60 and φ = 0 gives exactly the QRC input state for $s = 0.25$, Bloch vector $(0.866, 0, 0.5)$.

items: A qubit channel is an affine map of the Bloch ball into itself, the picture used throughout Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels).
Contraction of the Bloch ball is how a reservoir forgets: Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points).
The many-qubit generalisation, the Pauli expansion with $4^n - 1$ coordinates, is the reservoir's full internal state.

blocks.title: Locate a state
blocks.text: Find the Bloch vector of $(\vert0\rangle + i\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.

blocks.title: Angle of an input
blocks.text: What polar angle $\theta$ does the reset encoding give for $s = 0.25$? Check the Bloch vector.

blocks.title: Overlap from geometry
blocks.text: Use the Bloch vectors to find $\vert\langle0\vert+\rangle\vert^2$ and $\vert\langle0\vert1\rangle\vert^2$.
solution: $\vert0\rangle$ is $(0,0,1)$ and $\vert+\rangle$ is $(1,0,0)$: dot product 0, so the overlap is $(1+0)/2 = 1/2$.
$\vert1\rangle$ is $(0,0,-1)$: dot product $-1$, overlap $(1-1)/2 = 0$. Antipodal points are orthogonal states.
